title: A pricing page for a recruiting firm
metaTitle: A recruiting firm pricing page that shows fit
excerpt: Show what a search fee includes, what it leaves out, and how to brief the search. The page is for fit, not for arithmetic.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads, a still life standing in for a fee page that should show its contents plainly.
caption: What is in the vessel should be obvious before anyone asks. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a recruiting firm publish its fees?
faqs.answer: Publish the shape of the fee even when the final amount depends on the role. Say whether the search is retained, contingent, or a fixed engagement, when payment is triggered, and what compensation the fee is based on. A page that only says "custom quote" does not give a hiring manager enough to judge fit.

faqs.question: What should a search fee page list as included and excluded?
faqs.answer: Inclusions should name the work in the order a search happens, such as a scorecard, a capped shortlist, and a named person who stays on the search. Exclusions should use the same size type and cover real later invoices, such as advertising, assessments, or travel. Only list an exclusion you will actually enforce.

faqs.question: What should the pricing page ask the visitor to do next?
faqs.answer: Ask them to brief the search, not to request a quote you have already described. The next screen should collect the role and whether they have run this search before, and it should repeat the fee shape in one sentence. Do not promise a proposal on that call unless that is truly the next step.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A recruiting firm pricing page is where a hiring manager who has been burned before judges fit. They are not there to do arithmetic. They want to know what the fee includes, what it does not include, and how to brief the search. If the page says only "custom quote," they assume the number will move after they have invested another meeting. Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether a page gives a substantial, complete description of the topic, and whether a reader leaves knowing enough to take the next step. A fee page that hides the shape fails both questions.

Say the shape in the first screen. Retained, contingency, or a fixed engagement. What triggers payment. What is inside the work. What is a separate invoice. Then give one action: brief the search. The rest of the page can explain the edges. It should not be required reading before the shape is visible.

## Fit before the spreadsheet

The burned buyer has a private comparison already. The last firm quoted a percentage, then added an advertising line, an assessment vendor, and a replacement clause they found in week six. They are scanning for the same surprise. A table of tiers with invented names does not calm that scan. A plain statement of the shape does.

Write the opening as three lines they can repeat to their own finance lead.

- The type of fee: retained, contingent, or a fixed fee for a defined search.
- When money moves: at briefing, at shortlist, at acceptance, or only if they hire.
- The unit: a portion of the fee, a percentage of agreed compensation, or a stated amount for a stated scope.

You do not have to print a single number if the firm truly prices each search differently. You do have to print the shape. "Our fees are tailored" is not a shape. "Retained searches are billed in three parts, tied to briefing, shortlist, and accepted offer" is a shape, even before the amounts are filled in. If you do publish amounts or bands, define the compensation they apply to. Base salary, target cash, and equity are different bases. A buyer who has been burned will ask which one you mean. Answer on the page.

Leave the calculator off. A slider that multiplies a salary by a percentage looks helpful and trains the buyer to haggle the percentage instead of judging the search. If the fee is a percentage, say the percentage and the base in a sentence. If it is not a percentage, do not borrow the costume of one.

## What "included" has to name

"Full search support" is not an inclusion. Name the work a hiring manager can picture.

A scorecard written with them before outreach. Research limited to the kind of role you actually fill. A shortlist with a maximum count, so "a slate" cannot quietly become thirty resumes. Interview notes in a form they can reuse. A debrief after each round that says who is out and why. One named person who stays on the search from brief to offer.

Put the inclusions in the buyer's language, in the order the search happens. Do not sort them by how impressive they sound inside the firm. "Proprietary mapping technology" is an internal boast. "We write the scorecard with you before we call anyone" is an inclusion they can check.

If some searches include a market map and some do not, say which fee includes the map. A burned buyer treats a bundled extra as a later invoice. The page should make the bundle obvious. Two short columns are enough: in this fee, and billed separately. A paragraph that mixes both will be misread, because people do not read fee pages the way they read a letter. They hunt for the line that will surprise them.

## What is not included, said in the same voice

The exclusions are the trust. Write them in the same size type as the inclusions. A footnote is where the last surprise lived.

Common edges, if they are true for your firm:

- Job advertising and sponsored posts.
- Third-party assessments or background checks.
- Travel to the client's site.
- A replacement search, and the window, if you offer one.
- Candidate expenses.
- Work beyond the agreed role, such as a second seat that "came up along the way."

Only list an exclusion you will actually enforce. A page full of theoretical exclusions looks like a contract dumped onto the web. Pick the ones a burned buyer has already been charged for. If you do not charge for advertising because you do not advertise, do not invent the line to look thorough.

Say what happens if the search stops. If a retained fee is earned as the work is done, say that the early portion is not refunded when the role is cancelled, and say what work that portion paid for. If a contingent fee is owed only when they hire, say that too, including what "hire" means. A start date. An accepted offer. A contractor who later converts. Ambiguity here is how disputes start. The page cannot replace the agreement. It can stop the first conversation from being a trap.

## Do not hide a shape they will ask for anyway

Some partners worry that a visible fee will scare off a good client. The client who leaves because the shape is wrong was going to leave on the call, after you had prepared. The client who stays will brief a search that matches the fee. That is the fit the page is for.

There is a real limit. Do not publish a number your team will not honor. Do not publish a band so wide that it communicates nothing, such as "from five thousand to ninety thousand." A band is useful when it maps to a role you have already named. Plant leadership retained searches sit in this band. A single specialist role sits in that one. If you cannot defend the band, describe the shape and invite the brief.

Google's title-link guidance says each page needs a descriptive title element, and that vague labels do not help anyone choose a result. "Pricing" is a vague label. "Retained search fees" or "How a search is billed" tells a hiring manager they are in the right place. Google may build the title link from the title element, the visible heading, or other prominent text if those disagree. Make the visible heading and the title element say the same thing, in the same words. Do not stuff the title with every role you fill. A title that repeats "search, recruiting, talent, hiring" looks like a keyword list, which the same guidance warns against.

The heading on the page should be the one large title. If "Our philosophy" and "Pricing" are the same size, a stranger cannot tell which is the page. One heading. Then the shape. Then the inclusions.

## The brief is the next step, not a quote button

The action on this page is to brief the search. A "request a quote" button suggests the price is a prize you hand out after a form. You have already shown the shape. The brief is how you learn whether this role matches it.

The button can say "Brief this kind of search." The next screen should ask for the role title, the company, and whether they have run this search before. It should repeat the fee shape in one sentence so the brief is not a bait. If they are briefing a kind of search you do not price this way, say so on the services page and link there, once, in the exclusions or in a short note under the shape.

Do not add a second action that says "download our fee schedule" unless the file matches the page. A PDF from last year with different thirds is worse than no PDF. If finance needs a document, generate it from the same sentences the page uses.

Partners sometimes want a chat widget here. A widget that opens with "How can we help?" throws away the brief. If you use a scheduler, the event title should be the brief, and the confirmation should restate what to have ready: the role, why it is open, and what the last search got wrong. Do not promise a proposal by the end of that call unless that is truly the next step.

## How to check the page against a real invoice

Take the last three searches you billed. Put the invoice next to the draft page. Every line on the invoice should be predictable from the page. If the invoice has a line the page never mentions, add it to inclusions or exclusions, or stop charging it.

Then read the page aloud to someone who has hired through a search firm and does not work for you. Ask three questions. What would they pay, and when? What would surprise them on the invoice? What would they do next? If they cannot answer the first two, the shape is still buried. If they say they would email for a quote, the action is still a hallway.

Fix the sentence. Do not add a sixth paragraph of reassurance under a weak opening. The opening is the page for most visitors. A fee page that begins with a founding story will be judged before the thirds appear. Put the shape first. The story can wait, and on this page it probably should not appear at all.

## When the fee page is doing its job

You will know the page is ready when a new partner can send it before a call without a covering essay. The buyer who is a fit will brief the search. The buyer who wanted a contingent pile of resumes will see a retained shape and go elsewhere. That is a successful page, not a lost lead.

The fee still needs a sibling. A shape with no named offers looks like a rate card for unnamed work. Read [how each search offer should state its boundary](/blog/the-services-page-a-recruiting-firm-actually-needs) before you publish the fee on its own.

If you want a second pair of eyes on the structure of a fee page, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the shape you are willing to say in public. The call is for that decision, not for inventing a number you cannot keep.
